title: Asking, answering, saying no
goal: Build questions with Norwegian's seven question words, and negate sentences with *ikke* — which goes after the verb, not before it as "not" does in "don't".
bekal: tell yes/no questions apart from questions with a question word
put *ikke* **after** the verb, not before it
answer with *ja*, *nei* and — this is the interesting one — *jo*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — På kjøkkenet
dialogs.intro: The shared kitchen on the second floor. Budi is frying something when a neighbor walks in with an empty mug.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jeg heter Budi. Hvem er du?
lines.id: My name's Budi. Who are you?
lines.literal: I am-called Budi. who are you?

lines.speaker: Lars:
lines.text: Lars. Jeg bor her også. Hva er dette?
lines.id: Lars. I live here too. What's this?
lines.literal: Lars. I live here also. what is this?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Det er tempe. Det er indonesisk mat.
lines.literal: it is tempeh. it is Indonesian food.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Det er veldig godt. Vil du smake?
lines.id: It's really good. Want a taste?
lines.literal: it is very good. want you taste?

lines.speaker: Lars:
lines.text: Nei takk, ikke nå. Jeg spiser ikke frokost.
lines.id: No thanks, not now. I don't eat breakfast.
lines.literal: no thanks, not now. I eat not breakfast.

lines.speaker: Lars:
lines.text: Jeg er ikke sulten om morgenen. Bare kaffe.
lines.id: I'm not hungry in the morning. Just coffee.
lines.literal: I am not hungry in the-morning. only coffee.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jeg drikker ikke kaffe. Jeg drikker te.
lines.id: I don't drink coffee. I drink tea.
lines.literal: I drink not coffee. I drink tea.

lines.speaker: Lars:
lines.text: Drikker du ikke kaffe? Er du sikker på at du bor i Norge?
lines.id: You don't drink coffee? Are you sure you live in Norway?
lines.literal: drink you not coffee? are you sure on that you live in Norway?

notes: **This is the spot that trips up English speakers most.** The word *ikke* stands **after** the verb, not before it: *jeg spiser **ikke*** — literally "I eat not". English puts "not" before the verb with a helper (*I don't eat*), so your hand will automatically write *jeg ikke spiser*. That's wrong, and it sounds very wrong to a Norwegian ear.
**Yes/no questions are made by putting the verb first.** *Du bor her* → *Bor du her?* There's no helper verb like English *do*. Just swap the verb and the subject.

**All question words start with hv-, and the h is silent**: *hva* → **vah**, *hvem* → **vem**, *hvor* → **voor**, *hvordan* → **VOOR-dahn**, *hvorfor* → **VOOR-for**. One sound habit sorts out six words at once.

**Dette** and **det** both mean "this/that", but *dette* points to something close and *det* to something farther away or already mentioned. To ask about an object, *hva er dette?* is the most natural.
**Det er godt** — the adjective *god* becomes *godt* because *det* is neuter. The full rule comes in Unit 12; for now just learn *det er godt* and *det er kaldt* as whole phrases.
**Bare** means "only, just" and is said **BAH-reh**. It's one of the words Norwegians use most in everyday conversation.

grammars.title: Seven question words that take you anywhere
body: Learn this table whole. With these seven words you can already ask almost everything a newcomer needs to ask.

head: Norsk
Say it
Meaning
Example
rows: *Hvor bor du?* — Where do you live?
*Når kommer du?* — When are you coming?

after: Three extras that are useful right away: **hvor mange** (how many, for things you count), **hvor mye** (how much, for things you don't count) and **hvor lenge** (how long). All three build on *hvor*.
*Hvilken* changes form with the gender of the noun — *hvilken buss*, *hvilket hus*, *hvilke bøker*. Noun genders come in Unit 4, so for now just use *hvilken* and nobody will misunderstand you.
⚠️ *Hvordan går det?* literally means "how goes it?" and is the everyday "how are you?". The answer is almost always *Det går bra, takk* — "it's going well, thanks".

grammars.title: Two kinds of question, two word orders
body: Every Norwegian question falls into one of these two patterns. Notice that **the verb always stands in second place** — something we'll take apart in the next unit.

head: Kind
Word order
Example
rows: *Bor du i Oslo?* — Do you live in Oslo?
*Snakker han norsk?* — Does he speak Norwegian?
*Hvor bor du?* — Where do you live?
*Når kommer bussen?* — When is the bus coming?

after: What's missing here is the important part: **there's no helper verb**. English insists on *do you live…?*; Norwegian just says *bor du…?*. If you think through English, throw out the *do*.

grammars.title: Saying no with ikke
body: One rule, and it applies to every ordinary sentence: **ikke stands right after the verb**.
after: In a question, *ikke* moves behind the subject: *Kommer du ikke?* The rule stays the same — it follows the verb **and** the subject, never comes before them.

⚠️ The only place where *ikke* jumps **in front of** the verb is inside a subordinate clause (*fordi jeg **ikke** kommer*). That's a big trap waiting in Unit 18; for now it's enough to know the exception exists.

blocks.text: Norwegian has **three** answer words, not two. The third, *jo*, has no direct English equivalent, and that's exactly why it's worth learning from the start.

The rule is simple: if the question **contains a negative** and your answer **contradicts it**, use *jo*, not *ja*. English handles this with stress and extra words ("Yes, I *do*!"); Norwegian has one special word for it — just like French *si* or German *doch*.

blocks.title: Polite short answers
items: *Ja takk* — "yes, please", to accept an offer. Not just *ja*; that sounds blunt.
*Nei takk* — "no, thank you", to decline. Just as important.
*Det går bra* — "that's fine" / "no problem", an all-purpose answer.
*Kanskje* (**KAHN-sheh**) — "maybe", the polite escape when you don't want to decide yet.

sections.title: Eye training: one sentence, four forms

blocks.text: Read each row aloud from left to right. What you're training here isn't vocabulary but the habit of putting *ikke* in the right place.

blocks.title: A quick self-test
items: Take any five sentences from Unit 1, negate them all, then turn them into questions. If your hand writes *ikke* before the verb even once, start again from the top.
Say them as you write. The sound of *ikke* — **IK-keh**, with the *k* held — sticks in the ear faster than in the eye.

exercises.prompt: Negate the sentences by putting *ikke* in the right place.
Fill in the right question word: *hva*, *hvem*, *hvor*, *hvordan*, *hvorfor*, *når*.
Put the words in the right order.
